title: Respect!
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: In "Respect!", Dave Stuart Jr. recounts how a spontaneous, half-joking classroom bit — saying "Respect" and having students shout back "MAD RESPECT" in unison — grew from a one-off gag aimed at impressing his principal into a genuine ritual that carried his classes through a difficult year. He describes introducing the call-and-response early in the fall, using it playfully rather than as a coerced routine, and watching it stick as a recurring source of levity even amid two oversized 35-student sections and several tough general-level groups. The piece closes with student writing samples from the final day's warm-up, in which Dave used "Respect" as the day's quotation prompt, showing in students' own often-hilarious words how the small ritual came to symbolize class cohesion and mutual regard. Stuart frames the anecdote as an example of what's good about teaching: simple shared fun, the outsized power of repeated words, and the organic, jagged way Belonging actually develops in a classroom.
points: A small, silly classroom bit — teacher says "Respect," class shouts "MAD RESPECT" — became a real cohesion ritual precisely because Stuart introduced it playfully rather than as a forced expectation.
Stuart credits the habit with providing "a source of light" through a genuinely hard year of oversized classes and difficult general-level groups.
Using the single word "Respect" as a final-day writing prompt let students articulate, in their own voices, how the repeated ritual had come to represent class unity and mutual regard.
The essay frames Belonging as something that grows in "jagged and organic ways" rather than through any single deliberate program — the ritual worked because it wasn't engineered to work.

Stuart traces the idea's origin to his brother-in-law's use of the same "respect" call-and-response in a non-teaching workplace, showing the practice traveled from outside education into his classroom.
quotes: You guys are going to do what you do, work hard, get after it, pursue the mastery, and I'm going to just say, real nonchalant, the word 'Respect.'

The thing is, the little habit stuck. It became a source of light in an often trying school year, where I juggled a couple 35-student class sections, a couple really tricky general-level groups, and the ever-present journey of being a teacher.

This quote is an inspiration for us all to engage in the class and keep pushing for double-sided respect. If you aren't pushing for MAD Respect, what are you even doing? Step up your game and go for it; you won't regret doing so.
The simple fun we can have — even amidst the hardships. The ways in which words, especially repeated ones, can do things much bigger than the intent of the speaker.
But one thing you have to take, from one colleague to another, is the deep feeling I have when I think about writing to you. That feeling, in a word, is Respect.
